name: Multiple and Mixed Valvular Heart Disease

clinicalPearls: Multiple acquired and congenital lesions can produce stenosis and/or regurgitation across one or more valves; rheumatic disease classically affects mitral, aortic, and tricuspid valves alone or in combination.
In multivalvular disease, derangements from the more proximal valve lesion can mask the full hemodynamic expression of a more distal lesion.
Reduced cardiac output from mitral valve disease lowers transaortic flow and can lead to underestimation of the severity of a coexisting aortic lesion.

Functional tricuspid regurgitation accompanying significant mitral valve disease is one of the most common forms of multivalve disease; the tricuspid leaflets are morphologically normal and TR arises from right ventricular and annular dilation.

Onset of atrial fibrillation can be especially deleterious in rheumatic mitral plus aortic disease: loss of atrial systole can critically reduce cardiac output and raise left atrial and LV diastolic pressures.
When AR or MR is the dominant lesion in mixed aortic or mitral disease, the LV is dilated; when AS or MS predominates, LV chamber size is normal or small.

Secondary (functional) MR complicating severe AS reflects altered LV geometry and systolic leaflet tethering with normal leaflets and chordae; it may improve after relief of afterload with valve replacement.
Persistent significant secondary MR after aortic valve replacement is associated with impaired functional outcomes and reduced survival.
Severe mitral annular calcification can cause both regurgitation (reduced systolic annular shortening) and mild-to-moderate stenosis (calcium extending onto the leaflets restricting opening).
An early ejection click, typical of bicuspid aortic valve in young adults, is often absent in congenital mixed AS and AR.
Patients with multiple or mixed valve disease may become symptomatic earlier than those with isolated single-valve lesions, sometimes even with only moderate individual lesions.
Palpitations suggesting AF can flag clinically unsuspected mitral valve disease as an important component of the presentation.
harrison.pathophysiology: In multivalvular heart disease the hemodynamic effects of a proximal valve lesion can mask those of a more distal lesion. With combined rheumatic mitral and aortic disease, the reduced cardiac output imposed by mitral disease lessens the apparent severity of the aortic lesion, while AF arising during mitral stenosis can abruptly worsen previously silent aortic disease. Reactive pulmonary vascular disease acts as a secondary obstructive lesion in series, and as cardiac output falls with progressive tricuspid disease, associated mitral or aortic disease may be underestimated. Functional TR follows right ventricular and annular dilation with morphologically normal leaflets, producing large systolic c-v waves in the RA pressure pulse whose height depends on RA compliance and regurgitant volume; advanced chronic severe TR ventricularizes the RA waveform. In MS with concomitant AR, enhanced LV filling raises diastolic pressure depending on chamber compliance. Secondary MR in severe AS arises from LV remodeling and leaflet tethering under high systolic pressures. In mixed AS/AR, augmented transvalvular systolic velocities inflate the Doppler gradient and murmur intensity relative to true orifice size, and the Gorlin formula is inaccurate. In mixed mitral disease, the elevated mitral E-wave velocity in severe MR may not reflect any contribution of associated MS to LA hypertension. Noncompliant, nondilated, concentrically hypertrophied ventricles (as in significant AS, radiation heart disease, cardiac amyloid, or obesity/diabetes cardiomyopathy) tolerate acute volume loads poorly, so sudden AR causes rapid rise in LV diastolic pressure and severe heart failure.
additionalDifferentials: Patent ductus arteriosus (continuous murmur mimicking combined AS and AR systolic-diastolic murmurs)
Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm (continuous murmur, often after acute chest pain)
Isolated single-valve lesion with falsely overestimated or underestimated severity due to a masked second lesion
Pulmonary hypertension or right-sided valve disease underlying ECG signs of right heart abnormality in a left-sided valve lesion
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography as the principal modality, assessing valve morphology and function, calcification, chamber size, wall thickness, biventricular function, estimated PA systolic pressure, and great-vessel dimensions
Transesophageal echocardiography for more accurate valve (especially mitral) assessment and when infective endocarditis is suspected
Exercise testing with or without echocardiography when symptoms exceed resting TTE findings
Cardiac MR for additional anatomic and physiologic data when echocardiography is suboptimal (less suited to valve morphology)
Cardiac CT for intracardiac structures in complicated IE and for planning transcatheter valve implantation; coronary CT angiography as a noninvasive coronary assessment

Right and left heart catheterization to characterize individual lesion contributions, measure PA pressures, and calculate pulmonary vascular resistance, strongly recommended when clinical and noninvasive findings are discrepant in a symptomatic patient

ECG for ventricular hypertrophy/atrial enlargement and right-sided signs; chest x-ray for chamber enlargement, valve/annular calcification, pulmonary vascular changes (Kerley B lines, enlarged azygos vein indicating RA hypertension)
redFlags: Abrupt development of acute aortic regurgitation (e.g., from IE or paravalvular leak after AVR/TAVI) in a noncompliant, nondilated, hypertrophied LV, causing rapid rise in diastolic pressure and severe heart failure
New atrial fibrillation in moderate mitral disease precipitating heart failure when severe aortic disease coexists
Significant paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter AVR (risk factor for short- to intermediate-term death)
Symptoms of right heart failure (abdominal fullness/bloating, edema, ascites) signaling advanced disease
ECG or chest x-ray signs of pulmonary hypertension or RA hypertension in a patient with left-sided valve disease
harrison.prognosis: Natural history is usually driven by the dominant valve lesion; for moderate mixed AS/AR in which stenosis dominates, the course tends to parallel isolated severe AS. Patients with multiple or mixed disease may develop limiting symptoms or physiologic impairment even with only moderate lesions. Persistent significant secondary MR after AVR carries worse functional outcomes and survival, and significant paravalvular regurgitation after transcatheter AVR is a notable risk factor for short- to intermediate-term death.
pitfalls: The Gorlin formula is inaccurate in mixed aortic valve disease because augmented transvalvular flow from AR inflates the gradient relative to true orifice size.
Doppler-derived LV-aortic gradients and systolic murmur intensity overestimate true valve orifice severity in mixed AS/AR with preserved LV function.
A high mitral E-wave velocity in severe MR may be misread as indicating significant MS contribution to LA hypertension.
Low cardiac output from a proximal lesion (or AF) can mask the true severity of a more distal aortic or tricuspid lesion, leading to underestimation.
A mid-systolic outflow murmur is common in significant AR even without valve sclerosis/stenosis, so other signs of AS must be sought rather than assuming combined disease.
Combined aortic and mitral valve replacement carries significantly higher perioperative mortality than single-valve surgery, so the decision must be made carefully.
harrison.severityClassification: No discrete severity grading scheme for combined disease; severity is determined by an integrated clinical and noninvasive assessment that identifies the dominant lesion, whose grading and management recommendations are then applied, with attention to lesion severity, ventricular remodeling, functional capacity, and PA pressures.
management: Valve intervention directed by the dominant lesion, whether surgical repair or replacement or a transcatheter approach such as TAVI or transcatheter mitral procedures, addressing multiple valves at one operation where appropriate
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy for suitable rheumatic mitral stenosis
Medical heart-failure therapy with diuretics and afterload reduction, plus rate or rhythm control and anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, whose onset can be critically deleterious
Secondary antibiotic prophylaxis against rheumatic recurrence and vigilance for infective endocarditis
Serial echocardiographic surveillance of all valves, chamber size and pulmonary pressures, recognising that a proximal lesion may mask a distal one
Heart-team multidisciplinary assessment to determine the timing and mode of intervention, including right and left heart catheterisation when noninvasive data are discrepant
Management of pulmonary hypertension and referral for surgery before irreversible ventricular dysfunction develops
